standard_prerequisites.name: The axiom of choice used here
standard_prerequisites.statement: The form of choice in force says that every surjection between sets has a section.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the hypothesis, and the proof recalls its equivalent form.

standard_prerequisites.name: Suspension of a mere proposition
standard_prerequisites.statement: The suspension of a mere proposition is a set, and its two poles are equal exactly when the proposition holds.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the type on which the argument is run.

standard_prerequisites.name: Decidable equality of the booleans
standard_prerequisites.statement: Equality of the two booleans is decidable, so any proposition obtained by transporting it is decidable too.
standard_prerequisites.use: It produces the disjunction at the end.

core_obligations: Recall the equivalent form of choice and fix a mere proposition A (source lines 622-623).

Show that the map from the booleans to the suspension of A sending the two points to the two poles is surjective, by exhibiting a fibre over each pole and using that the truncated fibre is a mere proposition (source lines 624-630).

Apply choice to get a section of that map merely, and use decidable equality of the booleans to obtain the disjunction of the equality of the two values of the section and its negation (source lines 632-637).

Transport that disjunction along the injectivity of the section to a disjunction about the two poles, and identify the equality of the poles with A, which yields the law of excluded middle for A (source lines 638-645).

proof_roadmap.step: Fix the proposition and prove the two-point map into the suspension is surjective.
Apply choice and get a disjunction from decidable equality of the booleans.
Transport along injectivity and identify the pole equality with the proposition.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author labelled theorem at source lines 614-619 (book Theorem 10.1.14, Diaconescu theorem): the axiom of choice implies the law of excluded middle. The statement is a global implication between principles and gives no construction, and the proof (source lines 621-646) has to build the whole argument around one mere proposition A: the two-point map into the suspension of A has to be shown surjective, which needs a fibre over each pole and the fact that truncated fibres are mere propositions; choice then supplies a section merely, whose existence is used together with decidable equality of the booleans to produce a disjunction; and that disjunction has to be transported along the injectivity of the section and the identification of the equality of the two poles with A. Which form of choice is used, why the suspension of a proposition is the right type, and where decidability enters are all invisible in the statement.
